problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 16 & 0 \\ -1 & -5 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}],\,J=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-4 & a & ∗ \\ 1 & b & ∗ \\ 2 & c & ∗\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices above. Given that $A=PJ{P}^{-1}$ is a Jordan canonical decomposition of $A,$ find the value of $a+2c.$
worked_solution:
First, notice that the Jordan matrix $J$ may be written as a composition of Jordan blocks, as follows:

$$
J={J}_{2}(-1)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(2)
$$

So, we have

- a single $2\times 2$ Jordan block corresponding to $\lambda =-1,$ and

- a single $1\times 1$ block corresponding to $\lambda =2.$

Therefore, the columns of $P$ form the following chains: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{2}(-1) & : & {v}_{2}\overset{A+I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A+I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {J}_{1}(2) & : & {v}_{3}\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we obtain that 

- the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ of the eigenvalue $\lambda =-1,$

- the second column of $P$ corresponds to the vector ${v}_{2}$ such that $(A+I){v}_{2}={v}_{1}.$

Now, computing $A+I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 16 & 0 \\ -1 & -5 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 16 & 0 \\ -1 & -4 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, the matrix equation $(A+I){v}_{2}={v}_{1}$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 16 & 0 & -4 \\ -1 & -4 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 & 3 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 & 2 \\ -1 & -4 & 0 & 1 \\ 4 & 16 & 0 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-4){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & -6 & 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 24 & -12 & -12\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+4{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & -6 & 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we have ${x}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}({x}_{3}-1).$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}-2[\frac{1}{2}({x}_{3}-1)]+3{x}_{3}=2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=1-2{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}1-2{x}_{3} \\ \frac{1}{2}({x}_{3}-1) \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get  

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a+2c=-1+2\cdot 1=1.$
